result.question: Follow-up deep-research pass for PIIIX-org/portfolio.me on the four areas (3-6) that produced zero surviving claims in the prior adversarial verification pass, under an adjusted two-tier source policy (Tier A: normative specs/HIG/peer-reviewed/MDN/official docs; Tier B: named credentialed practitioners with cross-source consensus). Area 3: named visual style movements current 2025-2026 plus the separate anti-generic/templated-design discourse. Area 4: motion/interaction implementation (View Transitions API, FLIP, disclosure motion, chart animation, staggering, scroll-driven CSS vs JS, spring vs easing). Area 5: micro-interactions (Dan Saffer's framework, feedback/affordance signaling, optimistic UI, haptics/sound for web, and tracing timing-number folklore to Nielsen's 1993 source). Area 6: loading/perceived performance (skeleton screens vs spinners evidence, streaming rendering, optimistic/predictive loading, designed preloaders, CLS/Core Web Vitals).
result.summary: The question bundles four distinct research areas that each need a different kind of source. Rather than one query per area, area 3 is split into its two explicitly-separated halves (named movements vs. the anti-generic/templated discourse, since the deliverable treats these as separate and the meta-question about documenting movements undermining an anti-template mandate hinges on the second half), and areas 4-6 each get one targeted query aimed at the specific named frameworks/APIs/metrics called out in the prompt (View Transitions/FLIP, Saffer's framework + the Nielsen 1993 folklore trace, and skeleton-screen evidence + CLS) so the search surfaces primary/authoritative sources rather than generic listicles.

results.title: Skeleton Screens 101 (Nielsen Norman Group)
results.snippet: NN/g's core practitioner-tier reference on skeleton screens: explains the mechanism (progress-indicator illusion, mental-model priming before content dumps in) and cites NN/g's own response-time research that waits with feedback feel 11–15% faster than unfed waits, plus the classic 1-second 'dead time' attention-drift threshold. This is the strongest identifiable-author Tier B source directly on skeleton screens vs. bare waiting — good for separating real NN/g findings from folklore restatements of them.

Essential counter-evidence for the folklore-detection mandate: shows the 'skeletons always beat spinners' claim is not universally supported even in Tier B practitioner research, with a plausible mechanism (novelty draws attention; skeletons work better in familiar, short-wait contexts).

results.title: The effect of skeleton screens: Users' perception of speed and ease of navigation (ResearchGate)
results.snippet: An actual controlled academic study (not a blog post) directly testing skeleton screens against alternatives on perceived speed and navigation ease, found skeletons scoring higher on both measures — the closest thing to a peer-reviewed/methodologically rigorous source in this space, and the necessary counterweight to the Viget result for showing the evidence genuinely conflicts rather than being one-sided folklore.

This is unambiguous Tier A — a genuinely normative, Google-published measurement spec — and the clean strong anchor the area's snippet asks for to contrast against the contested skeleton-screen evidence.

results.title: Optimize Cumulative Layout Shift — web.dev (Google)
results.snippet: Google's companion Tier A guidance on CLS avoidance mechanics: always sizing images/video via width/height or CSS aspect-ratio, reserving space for ads/embeds/iframes, avoiding inserting content above existing content, and preferring transform-based animations over layout-triggering property changes. Directly supplies the 'documented failure mode + concrete avoidance technique' shape needed for a CRAFT.md-style CLS entry.

results.title: Skeleton Screens vs. Progress Bars vs. Spinners (NN/g video)
results.snippet: NN/g's comparative framing of the three loading-indicator families and the conditions each suits (determinate vs indeterminate waits, full-page vs component loads) — useful Tier B corroboration of the 'match the pattern to what's loading' condition-of-use guidance, and a second NN/g touchpoint alongside the main Skeleton Screens 101 article for cross-checking exact claims before citing.

claims.claim: Nielsen's actual three thresholds are 0.1s (instantaneous feel), 1.0s (uninterrupted flow of thought), and 10s (limit for keeping user's attention on the task) — the commonly-repeated folklore chain conflates these, often attributing 'attention wanders' to the 1-second mark when Nielsen's article attributes it to the 10-second mark.
claims.quote: 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted... 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.

claims.claim: 0.1 second is Nielsen's threshold for the system feeling like it reacts instantaneously to the user, with no special feedback required at this speed.
claims.quote: 0.1 second is the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously

claims.claim: Between 0.1s and 1.0s, Nielsen states no special feedback (e.g. progress indicator) is necessary beyond the response itself, though the user does notice the delay.
claims.quote: No special feedback is necessary during delays of more than 0.1 but less than 1.0 second

claims.claim: Above the 10-second threshold, Nielsen recommends percent-done progress indicators showing estimated completion time, because users will otherwise want to switch to other tasks while waiting.
claims.quote: users will want to perform other tasks while waiting

claims.claim: The article is Nielsen's original 1993 usability research finding, later updated in 2014 — making it the primary source the '100ms/1s/10s' folklore chain traces back to, rather than a secondary retelling.
claims.quote: Original Publication: January 1, 1993 / Update: 2014

claims.claim: Jakob Nielsen's classic three response-time limits are 0.1 seconds (feels instantaneous, outcome feels user-caused not computer-caused), 1 second (keeps user's flow of thought seamless), and 10 seconds (keeps user's attention before mental disengagement/abandonment) — this is the actual, precisely-worded source of the folklore chain commonly repeated as '100ms feels instant, 1000ms attention wanders.'
claims.quote: 0.1 seconds gives the feeling of instantaneous response — that is, the outcome feels like it was caused by the user, not the computer. / 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought seamless. / 10 seconds keeps the user's attention.

claims.claim: Nielsen explicitly reaffirms in this 2010 article that the three limits, originally published in 1993, are unchanged and still apply, and notes they derive from human factors research that was already ~40 years old in 1993 — i.e., not web-specific research at all but general human perception/attention research.
claims.quote: The 3 response-time limits are the same today as when I wrote about them in 1993 (based on 40-year-old research by human factors pioneers)

claims.claim: Nielsen states the primary cause of slow response times has shifted from image download delays (the concern in his earlier 1997 writing) to server-side data processing or overly elaborate page widgets, implying the limits themselves are technology-agnostic human-factors constants rather than being tied to any particular era's tech stack.
claims.quote: complex data processing on the server or overly fancy widgets on the page

claims.claim: Nielsen claims a direct business/conversion impact from shaving response time even at the sub-second scale, i.e. even reductions of 0.1s below currently-normal response times can measurably lift conversion rates — though this specific claim is stated without a cited study or figure in the article itself.
claims.quote: When sites shave as little as 0.1 seconds off response time, the outcome is a juicy lift in conversion rates.

claims.claim: Nielsen's classic three-tier response time thresholds (0.1s / 1s / 10s) originate from Robert B. Miller's 1968 research and were popularized by Jakob Nielsen in his 1993 book 'Usability Engineering' — this directly traces the commonly-cited 'instant vs. natural pause vs. attention limit' framework to its actual source rather than treating it as pure folklore.
claims.quote: The article attributes these thresholds to Robert B. Miller's 1968 research, popularized by Jakob Nielsen in his 1993 book Usability Engineering.

claims.claim: The 0.1 second threshold is defined specifically as feeling 'instantaneous' and reinforcing a sense of direct control by the user over the interface — not merely 'fast'.
claims.quote: Any interface response that occurs within 0.1 seconds will be perceived by the user as instantaneous. It also enhances their sense of direct control.

claims.claim: The upper bound of noticeable-but-tolerable response time in Nielsen's framework is stated as 10 seconds (motivation drop), not 1 second — meaning the popular folklore chain '100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the limit before attention wanders' misstates the actual upper threshold, which is 10x higher (10s) in the original three-tier model as this source presents it.
claims.quote: Response times between one and ten seconds are noticeable to users, and while they remain focused on the task, their motivation begins to drop.

claims.claim: Between 0.1 and 1 second, users perceive a delay but tolerate it as a natural part of processing/loading, per this source's presentation of the framework.
claims.quote: In the range between 0.1 and 1 second, the user notices a delay but accepts it as a natural processing time.

claims.claim: A separate, unrelated 100ms figure is cited from an Akamai report tying a 100ms page-load delay to a 7% drop in conversion rate — a business/e-commerce metric distinct from (and potentially conflated with) Nielsen's perceptual 0.1s 'instantaneous' threshold.
claims.quote: According to Akamai report, even a 100 milliseconds delay in website load time can reduce conversion rates by 7%

claims.claim: The View Transitions API covers two distinct use cases: same-document (SPA) transitions between DOM states, and cross-document (MPA) transitions between page navigations — the latter was previously unachievable on the web.
claims.quote: The View Transition API provides a mechanism for easily creating animated transitions between different website and element views. This includes animating between DOM states in a single-page app (SPA), and animating the navigation between documents in a multi-page app (MPA).

claims.claim: Cross-document (MPA) view transitions were impossible before this API existed, establishing it as a genuinely new capability rather than a convenience wrapper.
claims.quote: Cross-document view transitions (i.e., across navigations between different pages in MPAs) have historically been impossible

claims.claim: The API's transition mechanism works via a pseudo-element tree that captures a static snapshot of the pre-transition state and a live version of the post-transition state, which is the technical basis for its shared-element/FLIP-style morphing effect.
claims.quote: ::view-transition-old() — A static snapshot of the old view, before the transition. ::view-transition-new() — A live representation of the new view, after the transition.

claims.claim: Cross-document transitions require an explicit opt-in via a CSS @view-transition at-rule and are coordinated through PageRevealEvent and PageSwapEvent, meaning they don't fire automatically on every navigation.
claims.quote: Transitions between different pages... Opt-in via CSS @view-transition at-rule... Managed through PageRevealEvent and PageSwapEvent

claims.claim: Shared-element continuity across a transition is declared per-element via the CSS view-transition-name property, which assigns which elements participate in the snapshot-based transition.
claims.quote: view-transition-name - "Specifies the view transition snapshot that selected elements will participate in"

claims.claim: Dan Saffer's book 'Microinteractions: Designing with Details' defines four components of a microinteraction: trigger, rules, feedback, and loops/modes.
claims.quote: In his brilliant book, ‘Microinteractions: Designing with Details,’ Dan Saffer breaks down microinteractions into four components: The trigger, the rules, feedback, and loops/modes. Each of these components are critical to building a successful microinteraction.

claims.claim: Triggers in the Saffer framework split into two categories: manual triggers (intentional user interaction, e.g. a button push) and system triggers (automatic, condition-based, e.g. a toaster beeping or a text-message chime).
claims.quote: Manual triggers happen when someone interacts with the product intentionally. These are things like the flip of a switch or push of a button... System triggers are automatic and occur when certain conditions are met. Your toaster beeping when your toast is done or the chime you hear when you receive a text message are system triggers.

claims.claim: Feedback in the framework is defined as the acknowledgment signal to the user, which can take the form of sound, visual cue, vibration, or movement.
claims.quote: Feedback: This is the verification of the microinteraction, the signal to the user that their action has been acknowledged. It can be a sound, a visual cue, vibration, movement or something else.

claims.claim: Loops and modes are distinct sub-concepts: a loop governs the duration/repetition of the interaction over time, while modes describe a shift in how the product typically functions (e.g. Do Not Disturb).
claims.quote: Loops and Modes: A loop determines the length of the microinteraction. It determines whether the interaction repeats or if it changes over time... Modes change the typical way things function and operate. Examples of this are changing a location in a weather app or setting a ‘Do not disturb’ mode on your phone.

claims.claim: This ZURB-authored summary was originally published November 16, 2016, on the Prototypr Medium publication.
claims.quote: ZURB3 min read·Nov 16, 2016

claims.claim: Dan Saffer's microinteraction framework (from 'Microinteractions: Designing with Details') consists of exactly four components: trigger, rules, feedback, and loops and modes — matching the framework the research question asked to verify precisely.
claims.quote: According to Dan Saffer, a former Head of Product Design at Flipboard and the author of "Microinteractions: Designing with Details", a microinteraction consists of four key components: trigger, rules, feedback, and loops and modes.

claims.claim: In Saffer's framework, the 'Trigger' component is defined as either a user action or a system-initiated event that starts the microinteraction.
claims.quote: The trigger initiates the microinteraction. It can be a user action (clicking a button, hovering over an element) or a system-initiated event (receiving a notification, reaching a milestone).

claims.claim: The 'Rules' component explicitly governs animation duration and the conditions for when the microinteraction starts/ends, not just sequencing — directly relevant to timing-guidance claims in area 5.
claims.quote: Rules define what happens once the microinteraction is triggered. They determine the sequence of events, the duration of animations, and the conditions under which the microinteraction occurs or ends.

claims.claim: The 'Feedback' component of the framework names three channels — visual, auditory, and haptic — as legitimate microinteraction feedback types, without qualifying which are actually implementable on the web.
claims.quote: Feedback communicates the results of the microinteraction to the user. It can be visual (animations, color changes), auditory (sound effects), or haptic (vibrations).

claims.claim: The 'Loops and Modes' component covers two distinct concepts: loops (repetition/evolution over time) and modes (context-specific variations of the interaction).
claims.quote: Loops and modes determine the long-term behavior of the microinteraction. Loops define how the microinteraction repeats or evolves over time, while modes create different variations of the microinteraction for specific contexts or conditions.

results.title: Neubrutalism is taking over the web — Michał Malewicz (Hype4 Academy)
results.snippet: The primary-source naming essay (March 2022, still the reference point in 2025-2026 retrospectives) by Michał Malewicz — the designer credited with naming both neubrutalism and, separately, glassmorphism/neumorphism. Exactly the 'named practitioner who names and defends a style' the brief asks for: argues neubrutalism is a reaction against sterile flat/minimal SaaS design, describes its defining mechanics (raw color blocks, thick borders, deliberately 'unfinished' typography, high contrast) and the aesthetic-fatigue condition that makes it the right choice. Tier B, single-author origin claim but widely cited as the trend's naming event.

results.title: Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/g (explicitly whitelisted in the source policy) treats neobrutalism as a defined pattern with best-practice guidance and a cited 2026 usability finding: chaotic/undisciplined brutalist layouts dropped task-success rates to 8-10% on information-heavy pages versus disciplined-grid brutalist layouts. This is the strongest candidate in this pass for a documented, named failure mode with something closer to measured evidence rather than opinion — directly answers 'characteristic failure mode' and 'condition under which it's the right choice.'

results.title: Web Design Trends 2026: What Actually Held Up After Six Months — Studio Meyer
results.snippet: Named studio's mid-year retrospective explicitly separating hype from shipped reality: identifies 'anti-grid brutalism' as an unpredicted counter-movement to bento grids, and calls out kinetic typography's characteristic failure mode by name — it 'appears everywhere as demos on Awwwards and Dribbble but rarely ships in production because animated text fights screen readers, search crawlers, and adds layout shift that destroys Core Web Vitals scores.' Also flags AI personalization breaking against GDPR and llms.txt/agents.json as an unexpected 2026 story. Practitioner consensus tier, but unusually specific and falsifiable (mechanics + failure mode + condition) rather than a generic trend listicle.

results.title: Awwwards Jury 2026
results.snippet: The jury roster for the award platform the source policy names directly ('Awwwards/CSS Design Awards jury commentary'). Useful as the anchor for jury-credentialed practitioners whose Site of the Day/Year picks constitute the closest thing to a curated 'what's actually current' signal for named movements; secondary searches should pull specific jury members' commentary on 2025-2026 winners rather than treating the roster page itself as the analytical source.

results.title: AI Slop Web Design: Complete Guide to Spotting and Fixing Generic Websites (2026) — 925 Studios
results.snippet: Named studio's field guide to the anti-generic/anti-template discourse specifically: defines 'AI slop' as sites that default to the same fonts, colors, and layouts because they're vibe-coded off templates, and frames the 2025-2026 backlash (tactile brutalism, organic/asymmetric layouts, custom illustration) as a direct response to that homogenization. Directly relevant to the brief's parallel question about what reads as 'templated' and the discourse on distinctive vs. homogenized design — though it reads more as practitioner opinion/marketing content than rigorous analysis, so the adversarial pass should check it's presented as such.

results.title: Brutalism category — CSS Design Awards
results.snippet: CSS Design Awards' own brutalism category page, offered as corroborating evidence that a named award platform (the other one explicitly cited in the source policy) formally recognizes brutalism as a distinct, currently-awarded style rather than a retrospectively-imposed label — useful as a naming/legitimacy citation, but the page itself is a gallery, not analytical commentary, so it needs pairing with actual jury-member writeups to support mechanics/failure-mode claims.

claims.claim: New-view snapshots in the View Transitions API are not static screenshots but live representations of the DOM node, which is why content like a playing video can continue playing during the transition.
claims.quote: While you can use the term screenshot for the old snapshot, the new snapshot is not a screenshot but actually a live representation of the node.

claims.claim: Cross-document view transitions are opt-in via CSS, and browsers without support simply ignore that CSS rule when parsing stylesheets, making the feature safe for progressive enhancement.
claims.quote: Browsers that don't support them will ignore the CSS opt-in when parsing stylesheets.

claims.claim: As of the article's writing, same-document view transitions were supported in Chrome, with same-document support coming to Safari (Safari 18), reflecting a real (partial) cross-browser support gap developers must design around.
claims.quote: Currently available in Chrome, with same document view transitions soon to be available in Safari.

claims.claim: Chrome documents a concurrency limitation/gotcha: only one view transition can run per document at the same time.
claims.quote: Currently, Chrome is limited to running one view transition per document at the same time.

claims.claim: The performance cost of the pageswap event/snapshotting is minimal because snapshot data is taken directly from the compositor (no extra layout or repaint), with pageswap causing at most two stale frames.
claims.quote: the impact of `pageswap` for example is two stale frames at most

claims.claim: Cross-document view transitions require an explicit CSS opt-in on both the departure and destination documents via the @view-transition at-rule with navigation:auto, unlike same-document transitions which use document.startViewTransition().
claims.quote: @view-transition { navigation: auto; }

claims.claim: Cross-document view transitions are supported in Chrome starting at Chrome version 126 (and Edge 126); Safari added support at 18.2; Firefox support was not yet shipped as of this page's content.
claims.quote: Cross-document view transitions are supported in Chrome from Chrome 126.

claims.claim: Cross-document view transitions only work for same-origin navigations (identical scheme, host, and port) — cross-origin navigations do not get a transition.
claims.quote: Cross-document view transitions are limited to **same-origin navigations** only.

claims.claim: If the navigation itself takes too long (more than 4 seconds in Chrome), the browser skips the view transition and throws a TimeoutError DOMException rather than continuing to wait.
claims.quote: If a navigation takes too long–more than four seconds in Chrome's case–then the view transition is skipped with a `TimeoutError` `DOMException`.

claims.claim: To customize a cross-document transition (e.g. reading navigation direction) developers must register a pagereveal listener as a classic parser-blocking script in <head>, because the listener must run before the first render opportunity — async/deferred module scripts run too late.
claims.quote: The `pagereveal` event listener needs to execute before the first rendering opportunity. Therefore you must register the listener in a classic parser-blocking script in the `<head>`

claims.claim: As of December 2024, Chrome supports CSS scroll-driven animations (scroll() and view() timelines) safely for production use, Firefox supports them only behind a flag, and Safari does not support them yet (requiring a JS polyfill for cross-browser parity).
claims.quote: You can safely use scroll-driven animations in Chrome as of December 2024. Firefox supports them, too, though you'll need to enable a flag. Not yet, but don't worry — you can still offer a seamless experience across all browsers with a polyfill.

claims.claim: Native CSS scroll-driven animations run off the main thread and are GPU-accelerated, giving a real performance advantage over JS-based polyfills/libraries, which do not get the same performance boost.

MDN states verbatim that ::view-transition-old() is "a static snapshot of the old view, before the transition" and ::view-transition-new() is "a live representation of the new view, after the transition" -- matching the claim's wording precisely, not an overreach. The "FLIP-style morphing" characterization is independently corroborated: Chris Coyier's widely-cited piece ("The Shared Element Transition API is FLIPping Cool," chriscoyier.net, 2022) explicitly frames the mechanism as automating the FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play) pattern -- the browser captures old/new geometry via the snapshot pair and interpolates ::view-transition-group's transform/width/height between them, architecturally the same idea as manual FLIP. Chrome for Developers' view-transitions docs corroborate the same old/new snapshot-plus-interpolation mechanism for shared-element morphs (e.g., thumbnail-to-full-image transitions). No contradicting source was found disputing this mechanism description. The API (same-document since 2023, cross-document since Chrome 126/2024) is current and not deprecated/superseded as of 2026. Checklist item 1 (overreach) is the failure point. The quote given ("static snapshot of the old view" / "live representation of the new view") is accurate as far as it goes — that's the old/new pseudo-element distinction. But the claim then asserts this static-vs-live dichotomy "is the technical basis for [the] shared-element/FLIP-style morphing effect" (i.e. the position/size interpolation). MDN's own companion guide, "Using the View Transitions API" (developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transitions_API/Using), explicitly locates that mechanism elsewhere: "height and width transitions have a smooth scaling animation applied. position and transform transitions have a smooth movement animation applied... This works because, by default, ::view-transition-group() transitions width and height between the old and new views with a smooth scale." The same guide frames the old/new split purely in terms of interactivity, not geometry: "The snapshot of the old UI state is a static image, so that the user can't interact with it... The snapshot of the new UI state is an interactive DOM region, so that the user can start to interact with the new content as it animates 'in'." So MDN itself attributes the FLIP-style geometric morph to ::view-transition-group()'s captured-geometry animation (a distinct pseudo-element layer), not to the static-snapshot/live-representation property of ::view-transition-old()/::view-transition-new() that the claim cites as the "technical basis." findings.claim: The View Transitions API covers two genuinely distinct use cases — same-document (SPA) transitions via document.startViewTransition() and cross-document (MPA) transitions between real page navigations — and the cross-document capability is not a convenience wrapper: true animated transitions between separate Document objects across a real navigation were literally impossible on the web before this API existed.

Cross-document view transitions ... have historically been impossible.' Chrome for Developers independently restates the same 'historically impossible' framing and confirms no prior API equivalent existed (Chrome 126+ only). Distinct from JS libraries like Turbolinks/Swup/Barba.js, which fake MPA transitions via fetch+DOM-swap within one document rather than a real navigation — not a counterexample. findings.claim: The API's visual effect is produced by a pseudo-element tree (::view-transition > ::view-transition-group(name) > ::view-transition-image-pair(name) > old/new) in which ::view-transition-old() is a static snapshot/screenshot of the pre-transition state but ::view-transition-new() is a live representation of the post-transition DOM node, not a screenshot — which is why running content such as a playing video continues playing through the transition — and this old/new snapshot-plus-interpolation model is the browser automating the manual FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play) technique.

findings.claim: Cross-document view transitions require explicit CSS opt-in on BOTH the departure and destination documents via `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` (distinct from same-document transitions, which use the JS document.startViewTransition() API); the feature is currently supported in Chrome and Edge from version 126 and Safari from 18.2, but not in Firefox natively as of these sources; it works only for same-origin navigations (identical scheme, host, and port), with no relaxation shipped as of the CSSWG's still-open cross-origin feature request; and because it is a CSS at-rule opt-in, browsers without support simply ignore the unrecognized rule during parsing, making it safe for progressive enhancement with no fallback code required.

findings.claim: Jakob Nielsen's original 1993/2010 three response-time thresholds are precisely 0.1s (feels instantaneous, no special feedback needed, outcome feels user-caused not computer-caused), 1.0s (keeps the user's flow of thought/train of thought seamless/uninterrupted), and 10s (the limit for keeping the user's attention on the task before it wanders/before users start thinking about other things or abandoning). The commonly-repeated folklore chain ('100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the limit before attention wanders') conflates these by moving the 'attention wanders' claim from the 10-second mark, where Nielsen actually places it, down to the 1-second mark.
findings.evidence: NN/g (Nielsen's own byline, restating his 1993 article): '0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously... 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted... 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.' A separate NN/g article gives the same figures in Nielsen's own words: '0.1 seconds gives the feeling of instantaneous response... 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought seamless... 10 seconds keeps the user's attention,' with 'after 10 seconds, they start thinking about other things.' Independent secondary sources (e.g. perfplanet.com) confirm the folklore chain genuinely circulates in the conflated ms-based form. Tagged TIER B per this pass's policy (NN/g is the named practitioner source, though it is reproducing Nielsen's own primary claim). Merges verified claims [8], [9], [10], all 3-0.

findings.claim: Whether skeleton screens improve perceived performance over spinners is genuinely contested, not settled folklore-busting in either direction. A Viget (Tier B) controlled study (N=136) found skeleton screens had the WORST average perceived wait time (2.82s) of the three conditions tested, versus spinner (2.41s) and even a blank screen (2.29s), despite identical actual load duration via matched-length GIFs. But a separate, peer-reviewed (Tier A) study (Mejtoft, Långström & Söderström, ECCE'18/ACM) found the OPPOSITE point estimate — skeleton screens scored higher than spinners on perceived speed — while its own authors explicitly state none of the differences reached statistical significance ('cannot show any significant differences in any of the comparisons').
findings.evidence: Viget: 'Average perceived wait time (seconds): Skeleton screen 2.82, Loading spinner 2.41, Blank screen 2.29,' methodology used matched-length animated GIFs to hold actual load time constant. Mejtoft et al. (ACM DOI 10.1145/3232078.3232086, corroborated via Umeå University's DiVA repository): 'The results of this paper cannot show any significant differences in any of the comparisons between the web pages,' despite skeleton screens scoring higher on average and spinner users completing tasks faster. Confidence downgraded to medium specifically because the two admissible sources disagree in direction and neither individual study's headline number should be read as proof; a companion set of overreaching claims drawn from these same two studies were explicitly refuted at 0-3/1-2 vote during verification (see Refuted section) and must not be reintroduced. Merges verified claims [11] and [12], both individually voted 3-0 as accurate reports of what each study itself found — the contested synthesis judgment is the analyst's, not a re-litigation of the individual facts.

findings.claim: NN/g (a named Tier B practitioner source) asserts skeleton screens improve perceived performance by (a) creating an illusion of a shorter wait via suggesting gradual page transition and (b) preventing users from assuming the site is broken — presented as NN/g's own design recommendation/opinion, not as the outcome of an NN/g-run controlled experiment. NN/g separately gives specific, checkable wait-time thresholds for indicator choice: no indicator needed under 1 second; skeleton screens or spinners appropriate for 2–10 seconds; progress bars strongly recommended over 10 seconds — a banding that implicitly follows Nielsen's classic response-time limits, which NN/g cites in the same article's references.
findings.evidence: NN/g: 'Prevents users from assuming the site is broken during loading' / 'Creates an illusion of shorter wait times by suggesting gradual page transition.' Same article: 'If a page takes less than 1 second to load, skeleton screens or spinners aren't necessary'; 'Spinners... are best used when the page takes 2–10 seconds to load... skeleton screens should be used with a wait time that's under 10 seconds'; 'Progress bars are strongly recommended for any page that takes longer than 10 seconds to load,' citing Nielsen's 1993 article in its references. Confidence held at medium (not high) because claim [20]'s wait-time thresholds were voted 2-1 (not unanimous) and its 'supporting quote' in the original source material was flagged by the verifier as a paraphrase/table dressed as a direct quotation rather than verbatim text — a sourcing-hygiene issue worth correcting if reused verbatim in repo docs. Both claims are correctly Tier B (NN/g's own asserted rationale/recommendation, not a controlled NN/g experiment). Merges verified claims [19] (3-0) and [20] (2-1).

findings.claim: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a normatively defined, officially measured Core Web Vitals metric: it is the largest burst of layout shift scores within session windows (shifts <1s apart, capped at a 5s window) across a page's full lifecycle, where each individual layout shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction. Google's published thresholds are 0.1 or less = 'Good,' greater than 0.25 = 'Poor,' with the interval between = 'Needs improvement,' evaluated at the 75th percentile of page visits (sites should have CLS ≤0.1 for at least 75% of visits to qualify as good). Composited transform-based animations (translate/scale/rotate/skew, running on the compositor thread) are specifically exempted from counting toward CLS, whereas animating layout-triggering properties like top/left/box-shadow/box-sizing does count and should be avoided.
findings.evidence: web.dev/cls: 'CLS is a measure of the largest burst of layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifecycle of a page' with session windows (<1s gap, 5s max) and formula 'layout shift score = impact fraction * distance fraction'; 'Good CLS values are 0.1 or less, poor values are greater than 0.25, and anything in between needs improvement.' web.dev/optimize-cls: 'sites should strive to have a CLS of 0.1 or less for at least 75% of page visits'; 'Composited animations using translate can't impact other elements, and so don't count toward CLS... Changing the top and left properties also cause layout shifts... Avoid animating using these properties.' Independently corroborated by the WICG Layout Instability API spec repo (transform/opacity animations run on the compositor thread and are excluded from the metric by design). Merges verified claims [13], [14], [15], [16], all voted 3-0, all Tier A official Google Core Web Vitals documentation — this is the strongest-sourced material in the entire pass.

findings.claim: Neobrutalism is a named, currently-active (2025–2026) visual-design movement, defined by NN/g as an evolution of architectural brutalism into digital UI, characterized by high contrast, blocky layouts, bold colors, thick borders, and deliberately 'unpolished' elements. Its documented failure mode: applied without balance or preserved hierarchy, the style's bold high-contrast aesthetic can overwhelm users and actively hinder accessibility (not merely a stylistic risk) — mitigated by retaining hierarchy through size/color-intensity variation and ensuring bold color choices still meet text-contrast standards.
findings.evidence: NN/g: 'Neobrutalism (or neubrutalism), an evolution of traditional brutalism, is a visual-design trend defined by high contrast, blocky layouts, bold colors, thick borders, and "unpolished" elements.' Same article: 'While neobrutalism thrives on bold colors, heavy typography, and sharp contrasts, without balance, it can overwhelm users and hinder accessibility,' with mitigation guidance to 'retain hierarchy through size variation' and ensure 'bold colors must meet text-contrast standards.' Corroborated in substance (not verbatim) by independent practitioner commentary (Medium: 'Brutalism to Neubrutalism: What it means for UX & A11y'). Confidence held at medium: this is a single named Tier B source (NN/g) for both the definition and the failure mode, with only loose secondary corroboration, not independent cross-source consensus in the strict sense the pass's own policy defines for upgrading confidence. Merges verified claims [17] and [18], both voted 3-0.

result.caveats: Coverage is lopsided by design of the verification process, not by researcher choice: Area 4 and the CLS portion of Area 6 are strongly evidenced (mostly unanimous Tier A), while Area 3 and Area 5 are thin — only neobrutalism (area 3) and Nielsen's three thresholds (area 5) survived, out of a much larger requested scope for each.
